title: Scaling with parallelism
hypothesis: Doubling the cores available to Spark gives at least 1.6 times speed-up.
conclusion: local[1]: 31.8s wall clock, 23.2s of work after removing 8.6s of fixed cost; local[2]: 18.3s wall clock, 17.8s of work after removing 0.5s of fixed cost; local[4]: 22.8s wall clock, 22.6s of work after removing 0.2s of fixed cost. Speed-up on the work component against one core: local[1] 1.0x, local[2] 1.301x, local[4] 1.026x. Doubling from 2 to 4 cores gave 0.789x, against the hypothesis's 1.6x threshold: not met. Sub-linear scaling is the expected observation and is what the numbers show; the window aggregations shuffle, and shuffling does not halve when the cores double. This is intra-node scaling inside one JVM, not distributed workers, and the 100 GB tier was not run - see the limitations, which also record that shuffle bytes and spill are absent rather than approximated.
limitations: The 100 GB tier was not run and is not estimated: Docker has a 5.27 GB VM here (ADR-0002).

Distributed workers were not used. Compose can start a Spark master and one worker, but with 8 host cores and ~3 GB usable for containers two workers would contend for the same cores and the result would measure scheduling overhead, not scaling. `local[N]` varies the same knob - cores available to the work - inside one JVM, so there is no network shuffle and no cross-machine spill. The numbers below describe intra-node scaling only.

Shuffle bytes and spill are not reported. They come from Spark event logs, which are disabled in this environment; enabling them per run and parsing them was out of scope for this experiment and the measurement is simply absent rather than approximated.
